Abstract
Antimüllerian hormone (AMH) is an important component within androgen receptor (AR)-regulated pathways governing the hyperandrogenic origin of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). In women with PCOS, granulosa cell AMH overexpression in developing ovarian follicles contributes to elevated circulating AMH levels beginning at birth and continuing in adolescent daughters of PCOS women. A 6-7% incidence among PCOS women of gene variants coding for AMH or its receptor, AMHR2, suggest genetic contributions to AMH-related pathogenesis. Discrete gestational AMH administration to pregnant mice induces hypergonadotropic hyperandrogenic, PCOS-like female offspring with high circulating AMH levels that persist over three generations, suggesting epigenetic contributions to PCOS through developmental programming. Moreover, adult-onset, selective AMH overexpression within hypothalamic neurons expressing gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) induces hypergonadotropic hyperandrogenism and PCOS-like traits in female mice. Both gestational and adult AMH induction of PCOS-like traits are prevented by GnRH antagonist co-administration, implicating luteinizing hormone (LH)-dependent ovarian theca cell testosterone (T) action, mediated through the AR in AMH-induced pathogenesis. Interestingly, gestational or peripubertal exogenous T or dihydrotestosterone induction of PCOS-like traits in female mice, rats, sheep and monkeys fails to elicit ovarian AMH hypersecretion, thus AMH excess
per se
may contribute a distinct pathogenic contribution to hyperandrogenic PCOS origins.
Keywords:
neuronal AMH, overexpression of AMH, developmental programming, PCOS etiology, animal models
Introduction
The gene encoding antimüllerian hormone (AMH) or Müllerian inhibiting substance (MIS), a peptide in the transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) family, is highly conserved across vertebrates. It, or its Y-chromosome translocated duplicate, is involved in determining sex in non-mammalian vertebrates, including birds, as well as multiple reproductive and non-reproductive organ functions in mammals
1
. In males, AMH is mostly produced by spermatogenesis-nurturing Sertoli cells in the testis between early gestation and puberty
1
. In females, in contrast, granulosa cells within ovarian follicles are the major producers of AMH from late gestation until reproductive senescence. More recently, AMH production has been identified outside the gonads, including in the brain
2
, pituitary
3
and in ovarian cancer originating from the fallopian tube
4
. AMH is therefore a multi-organ system regulator with functions well beyond those of reproduction.
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent endocrine-metabolic disorder in women diagnosed by at least two of the following three criteria, (1) biochemical or clinical hyperandrogenism, (2) infrequent or absent menstrual cycles and (3) polycystic ovaries or elevated serum AMH levels, excluding other endocrine abnormalities
5
. Circulating levels of AMH are elevated in >90% of women with PCOS, reliably predicting polycystic ovarian morphology
6
due to exaggerated follicle recruitment together with diminished polycystic ovary selection of follicles destined for growth
7
. Polycystic ovaries over-secrete AMH
8
, particularly in anovulatory women with PCOS
9
, likely combining with elevated testosterone to promote pre-antral follicle survival
10
-
12
with AMH inhibition of FSH-induced antral follicle growth
13
-
15
. Some
9
,
16
-
19
but not all
20
,
21
studies even demonstrate AMH over-production within granulosa cells from polycystic ovaries. A recent study, nevertheless, has functionally implicated high levels of androgens, alone, in stimulating ovarian follicle granulosa cell AMH production
22
. Together, these findings implicate ovarian follicle AMH oversecretion in the pathogenesis of polycystic ovary morphology.
Not all studies concur with AMH enhancing ovarian preantral follicle survival, however, instead providing contrary evidence for AMH inhibition of primordial follicle recruitment, preantral follicle survival and proliferation
23
,
24
. The action of AMH on primordial follicle recruitment, however, is indirect, since human primordial follicles do not express AMHR2
25
and thus AMH action must involve neighboring ovarian cells. In addition, Dilaver and colleagues
22
demonstrate AMH-induced arrest of antral follicle growth while maintaining follicle viability and retention of FSH-enhanced aromatase expression, consistent with longitudinal ultrasonography observations of the growth of antral follicles in polycystic ovaries stalling out and regressing prior to attaining follicle selection
7
. Such premature arrest of polycystic ovary antral follicle recruitment was predicted by Willis and colleagues
26
when they demonstrated premature aging of ovarian antral follicles from women with PCOS due to insulin-mediated precocious expression of granulosa cell luteinizing hormone (LH) receptors within medium-sized antral follicles, engaging premature luteinization
27
. In examining the role of AMH in the pathogenesis of PCOS, incongruent findings confuse current understanding. Elevating maternal AMH during a key gestational developmental window in mice generates subfertile, hypergonadotropic, hyperandrogenic female offspring exhibiting endogenous AMH oversecretion
28
for at least three generations
29
, thereby demonstrating transgenerational AMH-induced epigenetic transmission of PCOS-like traits. Potential genetic contributions to AMH-related PCOS in women have implicated loss of function in either AMH and AMHR2
30
,
31
. Although potentially reducing AMH inhibition of ovarian follicle recruitment and theca cell testosterone biosynthesis to promote polycystic ovarian morphology and ovarian hyperandrogenism starting in late gestation, respectively, diminished AMH signaling in women contradicts hyperfunctional expectations from mouse models
32
,
33
.
AMH determines neuroendocrine control of ovarian function
Neurons expressing gonadotropin releasing-hormone (GnRH) are among the first to differentiate during early gestation
34
-
36
. Their origin in the fetal nose is anatomically distant to functionally relevant locations within the maturing brain, thus necessitating migration of GnRH neurons along terminal nerve projections initially into the basal forebrain
36
and then caudally to a several locations, including the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH)
34
,
35
. Secretion of GnRH from neuroendocrine GnRH neurons into the MBH and hypophyseal portal veins drives anterior pituitary gonadotrope secretion of LH and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) into the systemic circulation to orchestrate ovarian function
37
. Non-neuroendocrine GnRH neurons located in extra-hypothalamic brain locations comprise the majority of GnRH neurons
38
.
AMH is expressed by embryonic neuroendocrine GnRH neurons from their inception
39
. Its expression continues during their migration to the differentiating hypothalamus and persists throughout gestation and postnatal life
39
. These recent findings highlight crucial roles for AMH in determining not only initial survival of neuroendocrine GnRH neurons, but also frequency and amplitude of episodic GnRH pulse release from the hypothalamus
39
-
41
. Recent studies in female mice employing genetic manipulation of AMH expression, with or without subsequent chemoactivation, producing enhanced or diminished AMH production, have provided novel insights into the roles of neuronal AMH in determining female reproductive function. Given AMH overexpression in ovarian granulosa cells from polycystic ovaries
9
,
16
and excess circulating AMH in women with PCOS, it might therefore be expected for neuroendocrine GnRH neurons in women with PCOS to also over-express AMH.
Therefore, to further examine the potential role for AMH in the pathogenesis of PCOS, this mini-review will focus on instances of enhanced and diminished AMH expression in specific tissues and the circulation as well as their associated PCOS-like traits in animal models and their associated traits in women with PCOS.
Enhanced AMH expression or elevated circulating levels of AMH
Discrete overexpression of AMH within hypothalamic neuroendocrine GnRH neurons
Employing 30-day chemoactivation of neuroendocrine GnRH neurons within the mediobasal hypothalamus of adult female mice, Silva and colleagues
41
demonstrated hyper-functional hypothalamic GnRH neurons exhibiting increased frequencies of episodic GnRH release. As expected, such GnRH hypersecretion elicited anterior pituitary LH hypersecretion within the hour of chemoactivation, leading to ovarian hyperandrogenism, elevated circulating levels of AMH, oligo-ovulation and polyfollicular ovaries. Any accompanying subfertility and metabolic dysfunction, however, was not ascertained. Interestingly, PCOS-like neuroendocrine and ovarian traits persisted for at least 8 weeks beyond cessation of chemoactivation-induced AMH overexpression
41
. PCOS-like trait induction was not due to AMH overexpression
per se
, but rather to its induction of LH hypersecretion. Administration of a GnRH antagonist coincident with the 30-day chemoactivation of AMH overexpression prevented induction of all PCOS-like traits
41
, implicating gonadotropin-driven testosterone excess, androgen receptors
43
and possibly estrogen receptors following local testosterone aromatization, in the molecular cascade underpinning PCOS-like pathogenesis.
Silva and colleagues
41
thus provide the first demonstration of adult-onset, neuroendocrine induction of PCOS-like reproductive traits in an animal model employing discrete and transient chemogenetic induction of GnRH neuron-specific hyperfunction: no developmental programming was involved. In addition, the extension of PCOS-like traits for at least 8 weeks beyond chemoactivation of increased GnRH release frequency allows for possible testosterone-mediated feed-forward loops perpetuating excess LH and neuronal AMH (likely from continuing hyperfunctionality within GnRH neurons), ovarian testosterone and AMH, in tandem with oligo-ovulation. Such feedforward loops occur in female rodents and in women with PCOS. Testosterone acting through AR diminishes estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) expression in the arcuate nucleus within the MBH
43
. Estradiol acting on ERα-expressing kisspeptin neurons within the arcuate nucleus increases progesterone receptor (PR) expression, enabling ovarian estradiol and progesterone to suppress GnRH pulse frequency with subsequent diminished pituitary LH release; these events provide negative feedback homeostatic control onto integrated functions between pituitary and the ovaries
44
-
46
. Hyperandrogenemia that reduces estradiol- and progesterone (ERα and PR)-mediated hypothalamic negative feedback perpetuates LH hypersecretion and ovarian hyperandrogenism, leading to enhanced ovarian follicle recruitment, increased granulosa cell AMH production, diminished FSH release and action, and ultimately impaired ovulation. In support of testosterone-driven diminished hypothalamic ERα and PR activity, increased estradiol and/or progesterone are required to effect negative feedback inhibition of LH in both women with PCOS
47
and in animal models of PCOS
32
, while anti-androgen administration normalizes LH negative feedback responses to progesterone administration in both circumstances
32
,
47
,
48
.
While not pursued by Silva and colleagues
41
in their hyperfunctional GnRH neuron-specific mouse model, testosterone excess also induces metabolic dysfunction in women with PCOS and animal models
32
,
49
. In an analogous fashion to testosterone actions diminishing ERα expression in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, testosterone accomplishes analogous diminution of ERα expression in the neighboring ventromedial nucleus
43
. ERα expression in the hypothalamic ventromedial nucleus enables estradiol-mediated regulation of metabolic homeostasis in females. Diminished estradiol-mediated ERα activity leads to obesity, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia
50
. AMH overexpression in female mice that induces a feed-forward loop to maintain ovarian hyperandrogenism may also perpetuate metabolic dysfunction, emulating that accompanying PCOS in women. Consistent with this notion, administration of flutamide, an anti-androgen, to normal-weight
49
, overweight
51
or obese
52
women with PCOS diminishes preferential abdominal fat accumulation and improves circulating lipid levels demonstrating AR mediated perpetuation of metabolic dysfunction in PCOS.
Adult female mice with global overexpression of AMH lack ovaries and reproductive tract
The relevance of genetically-induced AMH overexpression to PCOS is, however, confined to neurons and ovarian granulosa cells. Transgenic, global overexpression of AMH in mice chronically elevates circulating levels of AMH
53
. It prevents female reproductive tract development and impairs ovarian development such that newborn pups exhibit reduced numbers of ovarian follicles and oocytes which are lost prior to puberty, and by adulthood, no ovarian follicles remain
53
. There thus appears to be a limit to the degree of AMH over-expression if some degree of female fertility is to remain.
Administration of exogenous AMH to pregnant mice induces transgenerational PCOS-like traits in female offspring
Injection of recombinant human AMH into pregnant mice during a crucial gestational stage of development induces PCOS-like traits in AMH-exposed female offspring
28
. Similarly-timed testosterone injections also induce PCOS-like traits in female offspring
32
. AMH treatment increases maternal frequency of episodic GnRH release via AMH receptors on GnRH neurons, leading to subsequent maternal LH hypersecretion, ovarian hyperandrogenism and diminished placental aromatase, leaving female fetuses exposed to high levels of testosterone
28
. Since both pharmacological blockade of GnRH receptors on pituitary gonadotropes
28
and genetic knockout of androgen receptors on ERα-expressing kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus
42
prevent gestational AMH-induction of PCOS-like traits in female offspring (including LH hypersecretion and testosterone excess), gestational AMH excess induction of PCOS-like developmental programming is not a direct effect of AMH
per se
. Rather, it requires testosterone-driven, AR-mediated reprogramming of hypothalamic homeostatic control of female ovarian and metabolic function to enable gestational induction of PCOS-like traits and its epigenetic transgenerational transmission
54
. Importantly, maternal LH levels are not elevated during pregnancy in women with PCOS
55
, in contrast to AMH-injected female mice
28
. Nevertheless, maternal AMH levels are increased during pregnancy in women with PCOS compared to those without and thus raise the possibility that, in women, enhanced maternal AMH inhibition of placental aromatase activity coincident with persisting maternal ovarian hyperandrogenism both underly fetal programming of PCOS rather than, in mice, in which AMH-mediated maternal hypergonadotropism is crucial for induction of maternal hyperandrogenism underlying fetal programming, thereby and diminishing the likelihood of gestationally-administered GnRH antagonists ameliorating fetal origins of PCOS in women
28
,
55
,
56
,
57
,
58
,
59
.
Transgenerational transmission of hypothalamic androgen action, in turn, can be ameliorated by methyl-donor injection administration, as exemplified by methyl-donor normalization of estrus cycles, circulating levels of LH, testosterone and AMH, as well as body weight and metabolic dysfunction, in 3
rd
generation PCOS-like adult female mice, great grand-daughter descendants of dams injected with AMH during gestation
29
.
PCOS-specific pregnancy elevations of AMH and testosterone
No direct evidence has been obtained for translational applicability of gestational AMH excess induction of PCOS since AMH injections into pregnant female nonhuman primates have not been attempted due to the lack of recombinant macaque AMH. Moreover, it is unethical to perform such manipulations on pregnant women. Observations during human pregnancy, however, are consistent with elevated maternal circulating levels of bioactive AMH and testosterone
28
,
55
,
56
compromising placental aromatization
28
,

32

61

62

69

70
